raw_case_text:
The patient is an eight-year-old male born to non-consanguineous parents of Arab origin. He has three healthy siblings, and his pregnancy and delivery were normal. In January 2014, at the age of 5 months he presented to the Emergency Department of our hospital with acrofacial ulceronecrotic plaques which appeared initially at the age of 1 month over the cheeks and nose with subsequent development of similar lesions over the hands and feet. The parents reported exacerbations upon exposure to cold temperatures. At his arrival, he was hemodynamically stable and alert with no fever.
Physical examination on admission showed erythematous violaceous indurated plaques with central necrotic ulceration located over the tip of the nose, bilateral cheeks and ear helices. Similar lesions were seen on the knees and extensor surfaces of the arms (Figures 1A-C). There were no cardiopulmonary, gastrointestinal, genitourinary or ophthalmological abnormalities.
The patient was admitted for further investigation and treatment. During his hospitalization he showed signs of poor feeding, weight loss and failure to thrive. A nasogastric tube was inserted that facilitated his feeding, improving his weight. Despite topical wound care and systemic antibiotics including cephalosporins and vancomycin, systemic corticosteroids and antifungals, no improvement was observed, with new lesions appearing on the right hand and right elbow after exposure to cold. In addition, the patient developed unexplained febrile episodes with concurrent deterioration of the ulcers. Extensive laboratory workup was performed, as follows: skin and blood cultures showed no evidence of microbial growth (bacteria, mycobacteria and fungi). Cutaneous leishmaniasis was also excluded by smear and polymerase chain reaction. Blood work showed normal kidney and liver function tests moderate leukocytosis and thrombocytosis, normal hemoglobin level and no marked elevation of C-reactive protein or erythrocyte sedimentation rate. Anti-nuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, anti-Ro, anti-La, immunoglobulins, cryoglobulins and cryofibrinogens, C3, C4, C-ANCA and P-ANCA were all within normal limit. A biochemical assay for prolidase deficiency was negative, chest x-ray, abdominal ultrasound, were normal. Serology for human immunodeficiency virus was negative as well.
Two skin biopsies were performed, demonstrating epidermal necrosis, mild parakeratosis, mild focal vacuolar degeneration and apoptosis of basal cell keratinocytes., mononuclear lymphohistiocytic infiltrate surrounding blood vessels, eccrine glands and hair follicles together with fat necrosis and hyalinization suggestive of lipodystrophy. No thickening of the basement membrane was observed (Figures 2A,B).
Given the history of transient sterile pyrexias with pernio-like skin lesions, ulcerations and lipodystrophy, a disorder of type I interferonopathy was suspected. Trio exome sequencing obtained from peripheral blood of the patient and his parents was negative for mutations in genes responsible for different type-1 interferonopathies that were included in our differential diagnosis. Mutations in candidate genes which may explain the phenotype of our patient were not identified as well.

subjective.chief_complaint: An 8-year-old boy of Arab origin initially presented at 5 months of age with cold-exacerbated acrofacial ulceronecrotic plaques over his nose, cheeks, ears, hands, knees, and feet accompanied by recurrent sterile fevers and failure to thrive.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Beginning at 1 month of age, the infant developed cold-aggravated erythematous-violaceous indurated plaques with central necrotic ulceration over his cheeks and nasal tip that spread to his ear helices, hands, elbows, knees, and feet. Admitted at 5 months of age with poor feeding and failure to thrive (requiring nasogastric tube feeding), he experienced recurrent sterile febrile flares with new cold-induced acral ulcers that failed to respond to systemic cephalosporins, vancomycin, antifungals, and systemic corticosteroids.
subjective.past_medical_history: Born after a normal pregnancy and delivery to non-consanguineous Arab parents; three healthy siblings.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for cold-triggered acral/facial skin ulcers, recurrent sterile fevers, poor feeding, weight loss, and failure to thrive; negative for cardiopulmonary, GI, GU, or ocular symptoms.

objective.physical_examination: Alert and hemodynamically stable on admission; erythematous-violaceous indurated plaques with central necrotic ulceration over the nasal tip, bilateral cheeks, ear helices, knees, extensor arms/elbows, hands, and feet, with lipodystrophic changes; normal systemic examination.
objective.routine_investigations: Labs showed moderate leukocytosis and thrombocytosis with normal hemoglobin, normal liver and renal function, no marked CRP or ESR elevation, normal ANA, RF, anti-Ro, anti-La, immunoglobulins, cryoglobulins, cryofibrinogens, C3, C4, c-ANCA, and p-ANCA, negative prolidase deficiency biochemical assay, negative HIV serology, negative skin and blood bacterial/mycobacterial/fungal cultures, and normal chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound.
objective.advanced_workup: Skin smear and PCR for Cutaneous Leishmaniasis were negative. Two skin biopsies demonstrated epidermal necrosis, mild parakeratosis, basal keratinocyte vacuolar degeneration and apoptosis, perivascular/periadnexal/perifollicular lymphohistiocytic infiltrates, and subcutaneous fat necrosis and hyalinization suggestive of panniculitis/lipodystrophy (without basement membrane thickening). Trio whole-exome sequencing of the patient and parents was negative for known type I interferonopathy genes.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Cutaneous leishmaniasis (negative smear and PCR), bacterial/fungal/mycobacterial infections, prolidase deficiency, cryoglobulinemia, and systemic lupus erythematosus were excluded; based on cold-induced pernio-like acrofacial ulceronecrotic plaques, recurrent sterile pyrexias, and histological interface dermatitis with panniculitis/lipodystrophy, a clinical diagnosis of a genetically uncharacterized type I interferonopathy-like autoinflammatory syndrome was made (with negative trio exome sequencing for known canonical genes).
